sceneHappening: Run the race looking to Jesus; receive God's discipline; you have come to Mount Zion, not Sinai; do not refuse the one who speaks
summary: "Therefore let's also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let's run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don't grow weary, fainting in your souls. You have not yet resisted to blood, striving against sin." The readers have forgotten the exhortation quoted from Proverbs 3: "My son, don't take lightly the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines." "It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children... they indeed, for a few days, punished us as seemed good to them; but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness. All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed. Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord, looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it, lest there be any sexually immoral person, or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal." Esau "was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears." "For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched, and that burned with fire... But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable multitudes of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect, to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel." "See that you don't refuse him who speaks... Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens... Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can't be shaken, let's have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire."
whySettingMatters: The "cloud of witnesses" are the figures of chapter 11, pictured as spectators in an arena around a runner; the image is of an athlete stripped for the race, running with endurance. Jesus is the "author (archegos) and perfecter" of faith: the one who went first and brought it to its goal. The "joy that was set before him" may mean joy he set aside, or joy ahead of him, which he endured the cross for. Discipline (paideia) is the Greek word for the training of a child, and the writer reads the readers' sufferings as training from a father, not punishment; this is a hard teaching that needs care, since the letter has just spoken of the hardship of people who were not being disciplined for fault (10:32-34; 11:35-38). Esau's "no place for a change of mind" (12:17) has been read as Esau being unable to change his father's mind, or as his own repentance coming too late; the point is the seriousness of selling what God gives for a single meal. Verses 18-24 set Sinai (fire, darkness, a voice the people begged not to hear) against Zion (a festal assembly, angels, the church, God as judge, and Jesus). The "firstborn who are enrolled in heaven" are the church, and "the spirits of just men made perfect" are probably the faithful of chapter 11. The "shaking" (12:26-27) quotes Haggai 2:6; what can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken stays. The letter closes its main argument with the third solemn warning (12:25-29) and the image of God as "a consuming fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24).

people.note: The author and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross, despised its shame, and sat down at God's right hand.
Who sold his birthright for one meal and found no place for a change of mind.
Who at Sinai said, "I am terrified and trembling."
Told to run, to accept discipline, and to look for the kingdom that cannot be shaken.

questions: "Lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us." What do you think is the difference between a weight and a sin?
The writer calls suffering "discipline" from a father. What does that help, and what does it risk, in how we think of hardship?
Esau traded a lasting blessing for one meal. What small present satisfactions tempt you to do the same?
Sinai and Zion are set side by side. What does the letter want the reader to feel about where they now stand?
